formationLabel: Organized 4 December 1910 · LCMS Lithuanian Lutheran congregation · relocated from Chicago to 9000 S. Menard Ave. in 1974 · active
currentUse: Active Lutheran Church—Missouri Synod congregation at 9000 South Menard Avenue, Oak Lawn, Illinois. The official LCMS Northern Illinois District directory lists Zion, Pastor Valdas Aušra, and the Menard address; the congregation's current website identifies Zion Evangelical Lutheran Church as established in 1910.
summary: Zion is the continuing Lithuanian-founded Lutheran congregation organized in Chicago on December 4, 1910 and now worshiping in Oak Lawn. Its 2016 constitution preserves the original Lithuanian Evangelical Lutheran legal name, Illinois corporation number, and LCMS affiliation. Historical sources document a first wooden church at 35th and Emerald, with a 1910-versus-1915 acquisition/construction chronology that must remain explicit; a larger church acquired in 1922 at 22nd and Bell; and relocation to 9000 South Menard Avenue. A web-hosted transcription of Zion's 90th-anniversary program reports the last Chicago service on March 24, 1974 and renovation/dedication activity in 1975; because the mirror is not a verified Oak Lawn Public Library item page, its provenance is stated conservatively. The Oak Lawn institution and building are active and standing, but the exact street numbers, title chains, and later fates of both Chicago sites remain unresolved. Concordia Historical Institute catalogs two reels of Zion Chicago congregational records; no dedicated cemetery has been verified.

institutionLifecycle.formation: The congregation's constitution says it was founded on 4 December 1910 and preserves the original Lithuanian Evangelical Lutheran name. A 1961 anniversary account prints December 1, a minor date conflict retained in the record.
institutionLifecycle.jurisdiction: Lutheran Church—Missouri Synod, Northern Illinois District. Lutheran identity is continuous even though the congregation now uses the shorter Zion Evangelical Lutheran Church name.
institutionLifecycle.relocation: The last service at the Chicago church was 24 March 1974, followed by entry into the purchased Oak Lawn property. Renovation/dedication milestones continued in 1975; this was a relocation of the same institution, not a merger or new parish.
institutionLifecycle.currentVerification: The official LCMS Northern Illinois District directory and current congregation website identify Zion at 9000 S. Menard Avenue.

historicalNarrative.text: Zion is a Lithuanian Evangelical Lutheran congregation, not Chicago's Lithuanian Evangelical Reformed church or the later Tėviškės parish. Its 2016 constitution says the congregation was founded on December 4, 1910 and preserves its original name, Zion Lithuanian Evangelical Lutheran Church of the Unaltered Augsburg Confession, together with Illinois corporation file number 67321596. The constitution and current district directory place Zion within the Lutheran Church—Missouri Synod.

historicalNarrative.text: The first-site chronology at 35th Street and Emerald Avenue contains a real source tension. A 1937 Foreign Language Press Survey interview says the congregation organized in 1910 and acquired a church at that intersection. A visually reviewed 1961 fiftieth-anniversary history instead says a lot was purchased and a wooden church erected in 1915. Lituanus likewise dates dedication of the small wooden church to November 1915. The dossier therefore separates the 1910 institution from the 1915 building milestone and does not invent a street number.

historicalNarrative.text: Zion's first pastor was Jonas J. D. Razokas, whose service began in the early 1910s and continued to 1921. In 1922 the congregation acquired a larger church at 22nd Street and Bell Avenue. The anniversary account says it paid more than $13,000 for a brick church formerly used by Swedish Methodists. These sources establish the second Chicago site and institutional continuity, but they do not provide a verified street number, deed, parcel, or the later building disposition.

historicalNarrative.text: The congregation's postwar life included Rev. Jonas Pauperas's long ministry and sponsorship of hundreds of Lithuanian displaced persons. As members moved from Chicago, Zion purchased the church property at 9000 South Menard Avenue in Oak Lawn. A web-hosted transcription of Zion's 90th-anniversary program records the last service at the old Chicago church on March 24, 1974 and entry into the Oak Lawn building; renovations and dedication milestones extended into 1975. Because the direct library item page has not been verified, the transcription is used as a qualified program mirror rather than attributed as direct library custody. Thus 1974 and 1975 describe sequential relocation phases, not competing institutional endings.

historicalNarrative.text: Zion remains an active LCMS congregation at 9000 South Menard Avenue. The official Northern Illinois District directory lists the church, address, and Pastor Valdas Aušra, while the current congregation website retains the 1910 establishment identity. Concordia Historical Institute catalogs two microfilm reels of Zion Lutheran Church, Chicago records, providing typed archival custody without implying that every sacramental, corporate, or property record is present. No dedicated Zion cemetery has been verified, and the two former Chicago buildings' present conditions remain unknown.

conflictsWithArchiveRecord: The official constitution gives 4 December 1910; the 1961 anniversary article prints December 1. The 35th-and-Emerald site is described as acquired in 1910 by a 1937 interview but as a 1915 lot purchase/wooden church by the 1961 anniversary and Lituanus. The Oak Lawn move began after the last Chicago service in March 1974, while renovations and dedications continued in 1975; those years describe stages rather than different congregations.
gaps: Exact street numbers and title chains for both Chicago sites, the full 35th/Emerald chronology, disposition and present physical/interior condition of both former churches, complete corporate amendments, comprehensive records inventory, and any dedicated cemetery remain unverified.
